Where is Clarkstown, NY, and what does the town include?

Clarkstown is the most densely populated town in Rockland County, on the county's eastern edge with the Hudson River as its boundary. The town was created on March 18, 1791 out of Haverstraw. It covers about 47 square miles, of which roughly 38.5 are land and 8.6 are water, and the 2020 census counted 86,855 residents.

The hamlet of New City is the county seat and also the seat of town government, the Clarkstown Police Department, the county sheriff's office and the county correctional facility. New City accounts for about 41 percent of the town's population. The town also holds Bardonia, Congers, Central Nyack, Nanuet, Valley Cottage, West Nyack, Rockland Lake, Mount Ivy, the village of Upper Nyack, and the eastern part of the village of Spring Valley.

Four state parks lie inside the town: High Tor, Hook Mountain, Nyack Beach and Rockland Lake, along with Lake DeForest and Lake Lucille. The Palisades Center is of the largest malls in the world, and Clarkstown has more business districts than any other town in the county.

  • The New York State Thruway (I-87 and I-287) crosses the Palisades Interstate Parkway inside the town.
  • Clarkstown Mini-Trans runs five local bus routes.
  • NJ Transit's Pascack Valley Line stops at Nanuet, and Rockland Coaches runs express service to the Port Authority Bus Terminal.

Which school districts serve Clarkstown houses?

Several districts divide the town, so the address matters. The Clarkstown Central School District serves most of it, including New City, Bardonia, Congers and West Nyack. Nyack Public Schools serve Upper Nyack, Valley Cottage and Central Nyack, the Nanuet Union Free School District serves Nanuet, and a small slice on the western border belongs to East Ramapo.

High schools inside the town are Clarkstown North in New City, Clarkstown South in West Nyack, Nyack Senior High in Upper Nyack and Nanuet Senior High in Nanuet. Quote the district from the tax bill, since one street can sit in a different district from the next.

When are Clarkstown property taxes due, and what do they cover?

Clarkstown's Town Clerk, at 10 Maple Avenue in New City, collects town and county property tax for a calendar year. Full payment is due by January 31 with no penalty. The town's calendar lists the late fees and the quarterly option below.

Payment choiceDate or windowCharge
Full payment, no penaltyBy January 31None
Full paymentFebruary 1 to 28Additional 1%
Full paymentMarch 1 to 31Additional 2%
Quarterly paymentsJanuary 15, April 15, July 15, October 155% service charge
School tax, full paymentBy September 30None
School tax, lateOctober 1 to 31Additional 5%

The second to fourth quarterly installments are payable to Rockland County Budget and Finance in Pomona. The clerk says no official can waive a statutory penalty, and that a missing bill does not change what is owed. If no bill arrives in the first week of January or September, call the office for a duplicate.

The bill itself is a line-by-line list: county tax, town tax, an open space charge, fire district, water district, lighting district, sewer, refuse, ambulance and charges set by Rockland Green. A one, two or three family house counts as homestead, and anything larger counts as non-homestead. Fire districts vary, so two Clarkstown neighbors can pay different amounts.

How does the Clarkstown assessment calendar work?

The July 1 before a roll is the valuation date, and all properties are valued at market conditions on that date. March 1 is the taxable status date, when ownership and condition are fixed and exemption applications must reach the Assessor. The tentative roll is filed May 1, which opens the formal grievance period, and Grievance Day is the fourth Tuesday in May, when the Board of Assessment Review hears complaints and every application must be on file.

For a seller, the practical point is timing. A house sold in December still carries the status it had on March 1, and the next roll uses the next July 1 valuation. If you think the tentative figure is too high, collect comparable sales and photographs before May. The town also posts an online property assessment search for checking your record.

What does the Clarkstown certificate of occupancy mean for a sale?

The town describes its Certificate of Occupancy as the Town's assurance to a prospective buyer that a building is legally occupied and conforms to zoning and minimum repair and maintenance standards as of the issue date. One is required for an initial occupation, an alteration of an existing building, a change in use, or whenever a building permit has been issued. No certificate is issued while a deficiency or material violation remains uncorrected.

  • An altered, extended or enlarged building may not be used for more than 30 days after completion without a certificate.
  • A temporary certificate can be issued for a building in full compliance with zoning and near compliance with other rules, and it expires in 90 days.
  • Buildings that predate zoning and building codes, or permits that expired, carry an additional fee.
  • You apply at the Building Department, Room 101 on the lower level of Town Hall, 10 Maple Avenue.

Clarkstown does not require fence permits, but zoning limits residential solid fences and walls to 4 and a half feet along any lot line, and caps other fences at 6 feet unless they are set back from the lot line. Wood stoves and fireplaces always need a building permit.

Do rental rules affect selling a Clarkstown house?

They do if the house has tenants. Clarkstown's Rental Registry Law requires every owner of a one-family or two-family dwelling who rents it to register with the Building Department, unless the owner lives there. An approved registration lasts two years, and the town inspects registered rentals every two years, including smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and fire extinguishers.

Brokers must verify that a current rental registration exists before they list, show or offer a registered dwelling unit for lease, rent or sale. Penalties start at $4,500 to $6,000 for a first offense and rise for repeat offenses, with a separate weekly fine for each week a violation continues. If you inherited a rented house, ask the Building Department whether it is registered before you set a closing date.

How is a Clarkstown deed recorded in Rockland County?

The Rockland County Clerk records deeds, mortgages and satisfactions for Clarkstown. Documents must be originals in recordable form, legible, signed and notarized. The clerk lists a $45 filing fee and $5 per page, plus a $10 notification fee for deed filings and the current fees for the TP-584 and RP-5217 forms.

State law sets transfer tax at $2 for each $500 of price, paid by the seller, and the TP-584 is due within 15 days of delivering the deed. A 1 percent mansion tax is owed by the buyer on residences of $1 million or more. Ask your closing attorney early about the title search and the deed form, since a cash sale is recorded the same way as a financed one.

The 2020 census counted 86,855 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 89,659. New City makes up about 41 percent of the town.

When are Clarkstown town and county taxes due?

Full payment is due January 31 without penalty, with 1 percent added in February and 2 percent in March. The quarterly plan adds a 5 percent service charge and has installments on January 15, April 15, July 15 and October 15.

Does Clarkstown require a certificate of occupancy to sell a house?

The town requires one for new occupancy, alterations, a change in use, or when a building permit was issued. Ask the Building Department what is on file for your address before you list.

Do I have to register a rental house in Clarkstown?

Yes, if you own a one or two-family dwelling and rent it out without living there. Registration lasts two years and the town inspects rentals every two years.

When is Grievance Day in Clarkstown?

It is the fourth Tuesday in May, the day the Board of Assessment Review hears complaints on the May 1 tentative roll. The 2027 date is May 25.

Settlement goes back to the 1640s. Voters chose the name Freeport in 1853 and incorporated the village on October 18, 1892. The village started a municipal electric utility in 1898, and that utility still runs. Oystering gave way to commuting, and canals such as the Woodcleft Canal, home of the Nautical Mile restaurant strip, reach the Great South Bay.

  • Rail: the Long Island Rail Road reaches Manhattan in roughly 45 minutes.
  • Schools: Freeport Public Schools runs eight schools, with one high school.
  • Waterfront: boat access and canal frontage give many homes a marine setting, along with a flood obligation.

How does flood zone status affect a Freeport home sale?

For a large share of homes in the southern part of the village, flood zone status is part of the sale. The village flood management page explains that a premises may lie in or beside a FEMA special flood hazard area, and it states that a regular homeowners policy does not cover flood damage. A mortgage holder in a flood zone must carry a separate flood policy.

Freeport takes part in the National Flood Insurance Program and reports a 10% discount on flood premiums. Its Building Department keeps elevation certificates on file and has a certified floodplain manager on staff.

  • Ask the Building Department whether an elevation certificate exists for your address.
  • Look up the flood zone and base flood elevation on FEMA's site or through the village.
  • Remember the substantial improvement rule: if repairs or additions cost 50% or more of a building's market value, the building has to meet new construction standards.

What permit and code checks matter before listing in Freeport?

The village Building Department administers building, plumbing, electrical and housing codes, and it also regulates multiple residences and unsafe buildings. Permit filings now go through the village's OpenGov portal, and structural applications need signed and sealed plans.

A buyer's attorney can ask for proof that finished basements, extensions or extra kitchens were permitted. If something was built without a permit, resolve it before listing so the question does not surface mid-contract.

  • Pull your permit history from the Building Department at 46 N Ocean Avenue.
  • Confirm that any converted space has the proper approvals.
  • Check the village zoning map if the house holds more than one unit.

Which village services and exemptions go with a Freeport house?

The village runs more of its own services than most Long Island communities. Its departments include the Assessor, Building, Electric, Water, Public Works, Fire, Police and Recreation, and the Treasurer oversees both the Treasurer's Office and the Tax Office. The Village Clerk handles licenses, permits and village records and works with the Planning Board and Zoning Board.

A seller should tell the buyer which village services attach to the property and confirm what is billed separately.

  • Electric: Freeport operates its own electric department, and its rates and project bids are posted on the village electric site.
  • Water and sewer: the Water Department publishes rates and fees, a conservation and regulations page and an annual water quality report.
  • Sanitation: Public Works posts a pickup schedule by area, so the collection day depends on the street.
  • Emergency alerts: Emergency Management lists hurricane evacuation routes and a CivicReady alert sign-up.

Exemptions listed by the Assessor include senior citizens, veterans, limited income disability, clergy, home improvement, non-profit, business development and volunteer firefighters and ambulance workers, plus the STAR program. Ask the Assessor how a change of ownership affects any exemption you hold.

What are the village tax dates, and who records the deed?

Freeport residents pay a village tax separate from Town of Hempstead, county and school levies. The village Assessor's page lists its own calendar, and Nassau County runs a different assessment calendar, so call the county for its dates.

  • January 1: village final assessment roll published; the first village bill is due between March 1 and March 31.
  • September 1 to 30: second-half village bills are payable without penalty.
  • October 1: deadline for exemption applications and the taxable status date, by 4:30 p.m. in person.
  • November 1 to the third Tuesday in November: grievance window, closing at 8 p.m.

The deed itself is recorded by the Nassau County Clerk, who keeps the official index of real property ownership and offers online land record search. New York's transfer tax is $2 per $500 of price, paid by the seller on a standard sale and reported on Form TP-584 filed with the recording office.

More questions about Freeport, NY

Does a Freeport seller pay the New York transfer tax?

Yes, on an ordinary sale the seller pays $2 for each $500 of the price, and the TP-584 form goes to the county clerk with the deed. The separate 1% tax on residences of $1 million or more lands on the buyer.

Will flood zone status delay my Freeport closing?

It can if the buyer's lender wants flood insurance quotes first. Collect your flood zone, elevation certificate and any claim history early so the buyer can price a policy without waiting.

Where do I get a permit record for my Freeport house?

Ask the village Building Department, which handles permits and keeps elevation certificates. Its office is at 46 N Ocean Avenue, and permit filings now run through the village OpenGov system.

When must I file a grievance on a Freeport assessment?

The village window runs from November 1 until 8 p.m. on the third Tuesday in November, and the application has to be physically in the Assessor's Office by then. A postmark does not count.

Is Freeport its own tax collector?

Partly. The village bills its own tax, and Town of Hempstead, Nassau County and school district taxes arrive separately. Ask the village Treasurer and the county for payoff figures before you close.

Does Freeport have its own electric service?

Yes. The village Electric Department supplies power and posts rates and bid notices. The village history dates the municipal utility to 1898, and Freeport is one of two municipally owned electric systems in Nassau County.

Where is Clarence, NY, and how did the town grow?

Clarence sits in the northeastern part of Erie County, northeast of Buffalo, and it was the first town established in the county, in 1808. Tonawanda Creek forms the northern boundary with Niagara County. One of the first settlers, Asa Ransom, arrived in 1799 in the area now called Clarence Hollow, and the town takes its name from Prince William, Duke of Clarence.

Brick kilns, potash and gypsum mining brought industry by the end of the nineteenth century, and quarries followed. Today the town is partly suburban and partly light industry and farmland. It has no incorporated villages, and the town government offices are in the Clarence Center area.

  • The town covers 53.63 square miles, nearly all of it land.
  • The 2020 census counted 32,950 residents, a 7.4 percent increase over 2010.
  • Nearby towns include Amherst to the west, Lancaster to the south, Newstead to the east, and Lockport and Royalton in Niagara County to the north.

Which Clarence hamlets and schools matter to a buyer?

Clarence is a collection of hamlets rather than one downtown. Clarence Hollow is the main district in the southeast, Clarence Center sits near the middle of town around Goodrich Road and Clarence Center Road, and Harris Hill occupies the southwest corner. Swormville, Millersport and East Amherst lie along the western and northern borders and extend into neighboring towns. Spaulding Lake is an upscale housing project built around a former quarry north of Main Street, and Rock Oak Estates is a 55-plus community on Main Street.

Most of the town is in the Clarence Central School District, with one high school, one middle school and four elementary schools: Clarence Center, Harris Hill, Ledgeview and Sheridan Hill. A portion of the town belongs to the Williamsville Central School District. Two Catholic parish schools serve kindergarten through eighth grade, one in Harris Hill and one in Swormville.

  • The ZIP codes in town are 14031, 14032, 14051 and 14221.
  • New York Route 5 (Main Street) crosses the southern half of the town.
  • Transit Road (Route 78) marks the west line, and Sheridan Drive (Route 324) ends at Main Street.
  • The Thruway runs just south of town and clips a small southeastern corner.

How do I challenge a Clarence assessment?

The town says a property should be assessed at 100 percent of full market value, and it gives owners a three-step path to contest the number. The informal review accepts applications from January 1 to March 28. You are asked to show reasonable evidence based on market sales, and the town warns against comparing unlike houses, such as a five-year-old house to a fifty-year-old one or a house in a different neighborhood.

The formal step is the Board of Assessment Review on Grievance Day, the fourth Tuesday in May, which will be May 25 in 2027. Form RP-524 is used only for that board and should not be used for the informal review. Owners who still disagree can ask for a small claims assessment review, and the town posts SCAR instructions and an assessment timetable on its assessment cycle page.

The town also runs an online Property Record Online System for looking up parcel data and the informal review worksheets, which become available after January 1. Check the record there for errors before you list.

What are the Clarence tax due dates and penalties?

The Town Clerk's office collects property tax in Clarence, from the Town Hall at One Town Place. Town and county bills go out by mid-January and are due on or about February 15. School bills go out by mid-September and are due on or about October 15. If your taxes are in escrow, you receive a receipt after the bank pays rather than a bill.

On May 1 a 7.5 percent penalty joins the levy, and 1.5 percent interest accrues monthly until unpaid taxes are sold in November, at which point the total reaches 18.78 percent. After June 30, unpaid town and county taxes move to Erie County Finance. School taxes carry a 7.5 percent penalty from October 16 to 31 and 9 percent in November, and unpaid school balances are re-levied onto the next town and county bill. Partial payments of any amount are accepted. If you sold a parcel, forward the bill to the new owner or call the Clerk so the office can locate them.

What should I know about Clarence permits before I list?

Clarence requires permits for new construction, additions, conversions, pools, decks, sheds, walls, reroofing, and for plumbing, heating, cooling and electrical changes, including generators. Fence and sign permits come from Planning and Zoning, and driveway permits come from the County, State or Town Highway Department. The Building Department is at 6221 Goodrich Road, and the Town Clerk collects permit fees.

The town's own FAQ speaks directly to resale. Work done without a required permit may hold up the sale of your property and may affect an insurance claim, and the town can issue a stop work order. Every permitted project needs inspections and a certificate of occupancy or compliance before the space is used, and the department says its officers average about 15 inspections on a new single-family house.

  • Plumbers working in town must be licensed by the Town.
  • The town keeps records of permitted projects, and copies are available through a Freedom of Information request.
  • Variance questions go to the Planning and Zoning Department.

If your file has gaps, ask for the records before you accept an offer. A buyer can then compare your paperwork to the house as it stands.

How does the Erie County Clerk record a Clarence deed?

The Erie County Clerk records deeds for Clarence parcels. The deed must be an original, signed and notarized, with a legal description and street addresses for all parties, since P.O. boxes are not accepted. A TP-584 tax affidavit goes in duplicate, and an RP-5217 transfer report is prepared on the state's site because its barcode cannot be reused from another transaction.

Fees are a $45 statutory recording fee, $5 per page, $10 to file the TP-584, and $125 for the RP-5217 on residential or farm property ($250 for other property). The seller pays New York State and Erie County transfer tax at filing. The combined rate is $4.50 per $500 of consideration, made up of $2.00 for the State and $2.50 for the County.

Owners aged 62 or older who have owned and lived in a one or two-family home for at least a year can claim a reduction to $2.00 per $500 by affidavit. A one percent mansion tax applies to residences of $1 million or more. Residential transfers also need a Notice of Sale or Transfer of Ownership form delivered to the Clerk at the time of transfer, and the finished original deed is mailed back to you after indexing.

How many people live in Clarence, NY?

The 2020 census counted 32,950 residents, a 7.4 percent increase over the 2010 count of 30,673. Clarence has no incorporated villages.

When is Grievance Day in Clarence?

It is the fourth Tuesday in May, which falls on May 25 in 2027. Use form RP-524 for the Board of Assessment Review, and use the informal review process earlier in the year if you only want the Assessor to look again.

Where do I pay Clarence property taxes?

Pay the Town Clerk at One Town Place, Clarence, NY 14031, by check, cash, mail or online. After June 30 unpaid town and county taxes move to Erie County Finance.

Do unpermitted repairs affect selling a Clarence house?

They can. The town says work without a required permit may hold up a sale and complicate an insurance claim, and a stop work order is possible. Ask the Building Department what a project needs to be closed out.

How much is transfer tax in Erie County?

The combined State and Erie County rate is $4.50 per $500 of price, paid by the seller at filing. Eligible senior owners aged 62 or older can reduce it to $2.00 per $500.

Where is Cicero, NY, and what is the town like?

The town covers about 48.5 square miles, and a large swamp, Cicero Swamp, sits in its southeastern part.

The town began in 1790 as a township in the Central New York Military Tract, separated from Lysander in 1807, and lost its western half in 1827 when that portion became the town of Clay. Interstate 81, U.S. Route 11 and Routes 31 and 298 pass through, and the reconstructed Erie Canal follows the Oneida River along the north line. A small corner of Syracuse Hancock International Airport reaches the southern town line, and Michael Airfield, a single-runway general aviation field, is inside the town.

Partial payments are accepted if nothing delinquent is owed, and the first payment must reach the office by the no-penalty date. When is the Gates tax bill due without interest?

Where is Chili, NY, and what kind of town is it?

Chili is a suburban town in the southwest corner of Monroe County, and its northeastern corner touches the city of Rochester. The town was cut from Riga on February 22, 1822, and it covers about 39.9 square miles, almost all of it land. Downtown Rochester sits roughly 7 miles northeast of the hamlet of Chili Center.

Both Interstate 490 and the New York State Thruway cross the town. The town's own communities include Chili Center, North Chili (home to Roberts Wesleyan University), South Chili along the Thruway, West Chili near Black Creek Park, and the rural hamlet of Clifton.   • The Thruway (Interstate 90) runs along the rural South Chili area.
  • Roberts Wesleyan University, with about 2,000 students, anchors North Chili in the northwest part of town.

How does Chili assess a house, and how do I challenge the number?

Chili says every property in town is assessed at 100 percent of market value, using a July 1, 2024 valuation date for the current roll. For the 2026 roll the valuation date was July 1, 2025. The Assessor sets value and runs exemptions, while the school boards, the County Legislature and the Town Board set the tax rates.

The yearly cycle is simple. March 1 is the taxable status date and the exemption deadline. The tentative roll is filed May 1, Grievance Day falls on the fourth Tuesday in May, and the final roll is filed July 1. The 2026 Board of Assessment Review met on Tuesday, May 26, so that date has passed, and the next one comes in May 2027.

There are three levels of review, and each one wants evidence.

  • An informal review with the Assessor, by appointment from October through March, may include an inside and outside inspection.
  • A formal grievance goes to the five-resident Board of Assessment Review on form RP-524. The signed original must arrive with five copies, and faxed or emailed applications are not accepted.
  • If the board's decision disappoints you, a small claims assessment review petition (RPTL-730) is filed with the Monroe County Clerk within 30 days of the final roll, for a $30 fee.

The Town of Chili Receiver of Taxes collects the town and county bill, and the school districts bill separately. Town and county bills are mailed at the very end of December and should arrive by the end of the first week of January. School bills go out at the very end of August and should arrive by the end of the first week of September. Homeowners with an escrow account get a receipt rather than a bill.

Paying by card at the Chili tax counter or on the town website carries a processing fee. Debit cards have a $3.95 minimum, and credit cards cost 2.45 percent with the same $3.95 minimum. Payments owed to the County Treasurer for delinquent taxes go through the Monroe County website, so check which office the bill names before you pay.

After a sale, the old bill belongs to the new owner. The town asks the seller either to return the bill to the Receiver with the new owner's name or to forward it directly. A new owner may also face an exemption recapture charge, which the Assessor sets as a one-time amount when the previous owner had an exemption the buyer does not qualify for. If you carried Senior, Veterans or Disability exemptions, tell your buyer before closing so the charge is not a surprise.

The Building Department enforces the Chili town code and the New York building codes, and it issues certificates of occupancy or compliance after a final inspection. A project with a permit is not finished until that certificate is issued. Permit applications go through the CloudPermit online system, and the department answers questions about zoning and planning approvals.

  • Fences need no permit unless the lot is in a flood zone or the fence sits in an easement.
  • Upgrading an electrical panel requires a building permit.

An instrument survey map is often requested at closing. Look through your own closing papers first, then ask the Building Department whether one is on file. The Monroe County Clerk is the next place to check.

What happens at the Monroe County Clerk when a Chili deed is recorded?

Every Chili sale is recorded at the Monroe County Clerk's Office, 39 W. Main Street in downtown Rochester. The county lists a one-page deed at $50 with $5 for each added page. Filing the TP-584 transfer tax return costs $5, the RP-5217 equalization form costs $125 for residential property (and $250 for other property), and each residential deed carries another $10 fee.

Transfer tax at this office is $4 per thousand dollars of price. That matches the state rate of $2 for each $500, which the seller pays, and it is due with the TP-584 within 15 days after the deed is delivered. The deed must be a dated original with grantor and grantee addresses, a legal description naming the municipality, the new tax number, original signatures and a notary acknowledgment. To record the same day, you must be in line by 4:30. A buyer who purchases for cash and as-is still goes through this same recording step, so your closing timeline depends on how complete your paperwork is, not on the buyer's financing.

It falls on the fourth Tuesday in May each year. In 2026 the board met on May 26, and the 2027 date will be the fourth Tuesday of that May, so file form RP-524 with supporting evidence by 8 pm that day.

The Chili Receiver of Taxes collects the town and county bill at Town Hall, 3333 Chili Avenue. Delinquent taxes go to the Monroe County Treasury, and the school districts send their own bills in September.

The town issues a certificate of occupancy or compliance when permitted work passes its final inspection. If you did work without a permit, ask the Building Department what is required to close it out before you list.

A one-page deed is $50 plus $5 per extra page, with $5 for the TP-584, $125 for the RP-5217 on residential property, a $10 residential deed fee, and transfer tax of $4 per thousand dollars of price.

What is Glen Cove's geography and history?

Glen Cove is bordered by Long Island Sound and, on its other three sides, by the Town of Oyster Bay. The Census Bureau lists about 19.2 square miles, though only 6.7 square miles of that is land. Its hills are part of the Harbor Hill Moraine, a ridge left by glaciers.

English settlers bought the land from the Matinecock in 1668 and called it Musketa Cove. Residents renamed the place Glen Cove in 1834, and steamboats and then the Long Island Rail Road in 1867 turned it into a summer resort. Wealthy families such as the Pratts and the Morgans built estates here during the Gold Coast era, and several of those estates now serve as schools, houses of worship and conference centers. The city's own historian notes that a state law made Glen Cove a city in June 1917, ending 250 years inside the Town of Oyster Bay.

  • Waterfront: over ten miles of shoreline, three public beaches and a municipal golf course.
  • Rail: the Oyster Bay Branch has three stations in the city, Sea Cliff, Glen Street and Glen Cove.
  • Health care: Glen Cove Hospital is operated by Northwell Health.
  • Schools: the Glen Cove City School District runs two K to 2 schools, two grade 3 to 5 schools, Finley Middle School and Glen Cove High School.

What drives Glen Cove's economy and daily life?

Glen Cove's economy moved from sawmills and clay digging to starch works, then to manufacturing in the 20th century. Photocircuits began making circuit boards in 1951 and employed 740 workers when it closed in 2007. Powers Chemco, which became Konica Minolta's Glen Cove plant, closed its factory in 2006. The Census now lists health care and social assistance receipts of about $409 million and retail sales of about $1.06 billion for 2022.

Census retail sales per capita come to $37,941, and the average trip to work is 29.4 minutes. Residents also enjoy parks such as the 40-acre Morgan Memorial Park, which looks out on Hempstead Harbor, and the 204-acre Welwyn Preserve with its trails and shoreline.

The department's own page has a section titled "Selling your home?" that tells owners to disclose improvements and say whether permits and inspections were obtained. Many lenders will not finance a purchase without proof of a final inspection for completed work.

  • Basement and cellar occupancy is prohibited under city code, so a rented basement unit is a red flag for buyers.

What rental rules apply to a Glen Cove house?

Code Enforcement says that owners of one or two family non-owner-occupied rental properties must register them under Section 168-65 of the city code. Failure to register can lead to a notice of violation and penalties.

Short-term rental is tightly limited. Under Section 280-45.3, renting a dwelling unit, a detached garage, a dock, a pool or other accessory space for fewer than 28 days is not permitted in the city. A buyer who plans to run a vacation rental from a Glen Cove house cannot rely on that income.

Code Enforcement also covers neighborhood standards such as unregistered vehicles, parking on lawns and sidewalk upkeep, and it posts foreclosure prevention resources for homeowners behind on payments.

The city assessment department estimates the value of roughly 7,000 parcels, and the county adds its own assessment records. Exemptions for veterans, seniors and STAR are the most common ones, and the city accepts applications from September 1 through May 1.

  • June 1 to the third Tuesday in June: grievance filing period, with Grievance Day on that Tuesday.
  • August 1: assessment roll becomes final.
  • August 31: last day to file certiorari and small claims review.

Senior exemptions reduce city and school taxes by 5% to 50% based on income, and the application is filed at City Hall, 9 Glen Street. The deed is recorded by the Nassau County Clerk, which keeps the official index of property ownership. The seller usually pays New York's $2 per $500 transfer tax, and Glen Cove's median value is below the $1 million point where the buyer's extra tax begins.

No. City code Section 280-45.3 bars renting a dwelling unit or accessory space for fewer than 28 days. Tell any investor buyer up front.

Do I have to register a rental house in Glen Cove?

A one or two family house that is not owner-occupied and is rented must be registered with Code Enforcement under Section 168-65. Registering before the sale avoids a violation notice.

Grievance Day is the third Tuesday in June, and the filing period begins June 1. The roll becomes final on August 1, and small claims and certiorari filings close on August 31.

The Nassau County Clerk records deeds for property in Nassau County and maintains the official index of ownership, with land records searchable online.

Ask the Assessment Department how a change of ownership affects your veteran, senior or STAR exemption. The city accepts exemption applications from September 1 through May 1 each year.

Can you sell a house fast in Elmira, New York?

Yes, but the speed depends on the route you choose and on the condition of the house. Owners in Elmira, the county seat of Chemung County, usually weigh three paths: a traditional listing, a sale handled on their own, or a cash sale to a buyer who takes the property in its current state.

A listing tends to bring the widest field of buyers, though it also brings showings, inspections and a lender's appraisal. A cash sale trims those steps, which matters for an inherited house, a vacant property, a rental with problem tenants or a home that needs work the owner cannot afford. Whatever route you pick, the city and county steps below apply to the paperwork.

What do the Census numbers say about Elmira homes?

The Census Bureau figures show a city of renters and owners in close balance, with housing values far below the New York average. That low price point shapes how sellers think about repairs, because a roof or furnace bill can take a large bite out of a modest sale price.

The city counted 29,200 people in 2010 and 26,523 in 2020, so the housing stock has been serving a shrinking population for some time. Sellers should expect buyers to compare condition closely and to ask for credits on deferred maintenance.

Where is Elmira and what shaped its housing stock?

Elmira sits in the south-central part of Chemung County, in the Southern Tier, a short distance north of the Pennsylvania line. It covers about 7.6 square miles and is wrapped on three sides by the separate Town of Elmira. The Chemung River runs east through the city, and Newtown Creek joins it at the southeast corner.

The city was incorporated in 1864 and grew as a canal and railroad hub. The Chemung Canal reached it in 1833, and the New York and Erie Railroad followed in 1849. Its population peaked near 50,000 around 1950. Factories grew up alongside the rail lines, and firms such as Hardinge (founded 1890), Kennedy Valve and Hilliard Corporation (both in Elmira since 1905) trace back more than a century. Elmira College sits inside the city limits.

  • Road access: Interstate 86 (the Southern Tier Expressway) meets the city at Exit 56, and state routes 13, 14 and 352 converge here.
  • Climate: the NOAA normals show about 38 inches of precipitation and roughly 42 inches of snow in a typical year, so roof, gutter and heating condition matter to buyers.
  • Schools: the Elmira City School District serves the city.

What changed in Elmira's economy and why does it matter to a seller?

Elmira's population peaked at 49,716 in 1950 and has fallen at every count since. The decline began in the early 1970s, when several large employers closed or relocated, and the 1972 flood then wiped out much of the downtown. Urban renewal removed riverfront buildings to create Riverside Park, and about 40% of the commercial space in the downtown was eliminated.

Census data show health care and social assistance receipts of about $643 million for 2022, against retail sales of about $357 million. Mean travel time to work is 18.7 minutes, and 81.9% of adults 25 and older hold at least a high school diploma. Ask a local agent or appraiser for recent Elmira sales before you settle on a price.

The city is also drawing up a new comprehensive plan, called Thrive Elmira, and its open house took place on September 30, 2026. Community Development lists a zoning update among its projects, so a buyer who plans a change of use should check the current rules.

How does flood risk affect selling a house in Elmira?

Flood history is a standard part of any Elmira sale. The city is built almost entirely in the Chemung River flood plain, and its own Public Works page lists the Chemung River, Newtown Creek, Diven Creek, Hoffman Creek, Heller Creek and the storm drains as flooding sources. It records floods in 1889, 1902, 1935, 1936, 1946 and 1972.

The June 1972 storm dropped 6.85 inches of rain in two days and damaged or destroyed roughly 5,000 homes. Since then the city joined the FEMA Community Rating System. By the city's account, that work removed 118 properties from the flood plain and saves policyholders 10% on annual flood premiums.

  • Check the FEMA flood zone for the address before you list, so you can answer the first question most buyers ask.
  • Gather any elevation certificate, repair receipts and insurance claim history.
  • Ask the city Public Works office for its flood information packet if a buyer asks about past water.

What city rules should an Elmira seller check first?

The city enforces New York State codes, its own Code of Ordinances and a zoning ordinance, and Code Enforcement posts permit forms, fee schedules and complaint tools. A few local programs are especially relevant to anyone selling a rental or an empty house.

  • Rental registration: an ordinance adopted November 23, 2009 requires every rental property in the city to be registered.
  • Rental certification: a companion ordinance of the same date requires certification of rental properties and sets out when certification can be revoked.
  • Vacant buildings: Code Enforcement keeps vacant building registration and exemption forms.
  • Sanitation: city garbage pickup is opt-in, and the Assessor's Office handles opt-in and opt-out forms, so confirm the status with the buyer.

Community Development also runs a Vacant Rental Improvement Program, an owner-occupied housing grant and loan program and a lead hazard reduction program. Buyers of older houses sometimes use these, so it is worth knowing they exist.

When are Elmira property taxes due and how do you challenge an assessment?

Three separate bills apply to a city house. According to the Chemung County Treasurer, the City of Elmira collects in two installments due May 15 and September 15, the Town and County bill is payable in full from January 1 to March 31, and Elmira City School District taxes are paid in two installments due October 31 and March 31.

The city Assessor's Office, at 317 E Church Street, publishes the assessment calendar and is closed on Wednesdays.

  • June 1: taxable status date, valuation date and the deadline to file any exemption.
  • July 1: tentative assessment roll filed.
  • Third Tuesday in July: Grievance Day, 4:00 to 8:00 p.m., before the Board of Assessment Review.
  • August 10: final roll, with 30 days after that for small claims assessment review or certiorari.

STAR and Enhanced STAR are handled through the state's Homeowner Benefits Portal, not the city office. The Assessor does not hold billing or payment records, so ask the City Chamberlain's Office for a payoff of any unpaid city tax before closing.

What happens at closing in Chemung County?

Deeds for Elmira property are recorded by the Chemung County Clerk at 210 Lake Street. The office takes recordings Monday through Friday until 4 p.m., accepts e-recording through approved vendors, and has deeds searchable back to July 31, 1967.

New York charges a transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of consideration, and the seller normally pays it. The seller or the closing attorney files Form TP-584 with the county clerk within 15 days after the deed is delivered. The extra 1% tax on homes of $1 million or more falls on the buyer, and Elmira's median home value is far below that line. For any county tax balance, the Treasurer's Office offers an online tax clearance request.

More questions about Elmira, NY

How fast can an Elmira house actually close?

The timeline depends on title, payoffs and whether anyone lives in the house. A sale with clear title and no financing contingency moves fastest, while inherited or tenant-occupied properties can add weeks for estate papers or notices, so start those steps early.

Do I have to register my Elmira rental before selling?

The city requires registration and certification of rental properties under ordinances adopted in 2009, so an unregistered rental can draw questions from a buyer's attorney. Contact Code Enforcement to confirm your status before you list.

Who sets the property tax bill on an Elmira house?

Three bodies bill separately: the City of Elmira, Chemung County with the town, and the Elmira City School District. The Assessor sets the assessment, but tax rates are not set in that office, and billing questions go to the Chamberlain.

When is Grievance Day in Elmira?

It falls on the third Tuesday of July, from 4:00 to 8:00 p.m. You file the RP-524 form with the Assessor's Office, and the Board of Assessment Review answers by August 10. Miss it and the next chance comes a year later.

Does flood zone status stop a sale in Elmira?

No, but buyers will ask about it. The city says its flood program saves policyholders 10% on premiums, so gather your flood zone, any elevation certificate and your claims history so a buyer can price coverage up front.
